name: Diamond
note: 100% carbon. Each carbon atom locks onto four neighbors in a rigid 3D grid, which makes diamond the hardest natural material. Pencil graphite is the very same element arranged in flat, slippery sheets.

name: Graphite (pencil 'lead')
note: Pure carbon in flat sheets that slide apart and leave a mark on paper. A single sheet one atom thick is graphene, one of the strongest materials ever measured.

name: Water
note: Two hydrogens and one oxygen. By mass it's about 89% oxygen, because one oxygen atom weighs as much as 16 hydrogen atoms.

name: Table salt
note: Sodium (a metal that fizzes violently in water) plus chlorine (a toxic gas) makes the harmless salt on your fries. Chemistry can completely change properties.

name: Sugar (sucrose)
note: Plants build sugar from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight, so every atom in it once floated in the air or the soil.

name: Glucose
note: Your cells' main fuel. Photosynthesis makes it, and your cells burn it with oxygen to release energy.

name: Baking soda
note: Reacts with acids like vinegar or buttermilk to release carbon dioxide bubbles, which make pancakes and cakes rise.

name: Vinegar (acetic acid)
note: Vinegar is about 5% acetic acid dissolved in water. The acetic acid gives the sour taste and sharp smell.

name: Chalk / limestone
note: Calcium carbonate. Sea creatures build shells from calcium and dissolved carbon dioxide; limestone and chalk are ancient seabeds made of their remains.

name: Rust
note: Iron combined with oxygen, with water speeding things up. Rust flakes off, exposing fresh iron underneath, so it keeps spreading.

name: Sand / quartz
note: Silicon and oxygen, the two most common elements in Earth's crust. Melt it and it becomes the base of glass.

name: Window glass
note: Mostly sand melted with soda (sodium) and lime (calcium), which lower the melting point. Values are approximate.

name: Pyrex-type glass
note: Borosilicate glass. Boron makes it expand very little when heated, so it doesn't crack in the oven.

name: Carbon dioxide
note: What you breathe out and plants take in. Frozen at −78.5 °C it becomes dry ice, which turns straight from solid to gas.

name: Ammonia
note: Found in many glass cleaners and the starting point for most of the world's fertilizer.

name: Bleach
note: Household bleach is a few percent sodium hypochlorite dissolved in water. Never mix it with ammonia or vinegar: toxic gases form.

name: Hydrogen peroxide
note: Water with one extra oxygen. It fizzes on a cut because an enzyme in your blood splits it into water and oxygen gas.

name: Rubbing alcohol
note: It evaporates fast and carries heat away, which is why it feels cold on your skin.

name: Ethanol
note: The alcohol in hand sanitizer (usually 60–70% mixed with water) and in many car fuels.

name: Caffeine
note: Blocks the brain signal that makes you feel sleepy. Coffee and tea contain it, along with water and many flavor molecules.

name: Aspirin
note: A pain reliever originally inspired by a compound found in willow bark.

name: Vitamin C
note: Your body can't make it, so it has to come from foods like oranges, strawberries and bell peppers.

name: Methane (natural gas)
note: The main gas burning in a gas stove. Cows also burp it out, and it's a strong greenhouse gas.

name: Propane
note: Grill and camping-stove fuel, stored as a liquid under pressure in the tank.

name: Gasoline (octane)
note: Gasoline is a blend of many hydrocarbons; octane is a typical one. Burning it with oxygen makes carbon dioxide and water.

name: Epsom salt
note: Magnesium sulfate crystals with seven water molecules locked inside each unit.

name: Drywall / gypsum
note: Calcium sulfate with water built into its crystals. It's the white core of the walls in most homes.

name: Ruby & sapphire
note: Aluminum oxide. A trace of chromium makes ruby red; traces of iron and titanium make sapphire blue.

name: Emerald
note: The mineral beryl. A trace of chromium or vanadium turns it green; iron makes the blue version, aquamarine.

name: Fool's gold (pyrite)
note: Iron and sulfur. Its brassy shine fooled gold miners, but it's harder and much lighter than real gold.

name: Cubic zirconia
note: Zirconium oxide, a lab-made crystal that sparkles like diamond for a fraction of the price.

name: Fluoride (toothpaste)
note: A tiny amount in toothpaste helps rebuild enamel so it resists acid from bacteria.

name: Nonstick coating (PTFE)
note: A long chain of carbon atoms fully wrapped in fluorine. The formula shows one repeating unit of the chain.

name: PVC plastic
note: Pipes, raincoats and vinyl records. The formula is one repeating unit of the long chain.

name: Plastic bag (polyethylene)
note: The most common plastic: a very long chain of carbon and hydrogen. The formula shows one repeating unit.

name: Plastic bottle (PET)
note: Soda bottles and polyester clothing are the same plastic. Formula shows one repeating unit.

name: Styrofoam (polystyrene)
note: Polystyrene puffed with air; it's about 95% air by volume, which is why it's so light.

name: Silicone
note: A flexible rubber with a backbone of silicon and oxygen. Formula shows one repeating unit.

name: Paper / cotton (cellulose)
note: Long chains of glucose units that plants use to build cell walls. Wood also contains lignin, which glues the fibers together.

name: Starch
note: Plants store energy as starch, another chain of glucose units. Iodine turns it blue-black.

name: Bone & tooth enamel
note: The hard mineral hydroxyapatite. Fluoride can swap in for the OH group, making enamel tougher.

name: Chlorophyll
note: The green pigment that captures sunlight. Notice the single magnesium atom at its center.

name: Green copper patina
note: Copper slowly reacts with air and water to form this green coating, which protects the metal underneath.

name: Laughing gas
note: Used by dentists to relax patients and to push whipped cream out of cans.

name: Ozone
note: Three oxygen atoms. High in the sky it blocks harmful UV light; near the ground it's a pollutant in smog.

name: Lye
note: A strong base used in soap-making and drain cleaners. It can burn skin, so it's handled with gloves.

name: Stomach acid (hydrochloric acid)
note: Your stomach makes this acid to break down food and kill germs.

name: Battery acid (sulfuric acid)
note: The acid inside car batteries and the most produced industrial chemical in the world.

name: MSG
note: Gives the savory 'umami' taste. Tomatoes and parmesan contain glutamate naturally.

name: Stomach-relief medicine
note: Bismuth subsalicylate. The bismuth can temporarily turn your tongue black, which is harmless.

name: Silver tarnish
note: Silver reacting with sulfur from the air or foods like eggs forms this dark layer.

name: Fluorite
note: A colorful mineral that often glows under UV light. 'Fluorescence' is named after it.

name: Air
note: By mass. By volume it's about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% argon, plus a little carbon dioxide and water vapor.

name: Blood
note: By mass. Blood is mostly water, so oxygen and hydrogen lead. Carbon and nitrogen come from proteins like hemoglobin, salt gives chlorine and sodium, and the tiny 0.05% of iron is what carries oxygen around your body.

name: Human body
note: By mass. Most of the oxygen and hydrogen is in water, which makes up about 60% of you. Trace elements like iron, zinc and iodine are tiny but essential.

name: Seawater
note: Mostly water, plus about 3.5% dissolved salts. Chlorine and sodium from those salts are the next biggest pieces.

name: Earth's crust
note: By mass. Oxygen is the most common element in the ground under your feet, locked inside minerals.

name: The Sun
note: By mass, approximately. The Sun turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second.

name: Steel
note: Iron with a little carbon added, which makes it much stronger. Recipes vary by use.

name: Stainless steel
note: Typical '18/8' grade. Chromium forms an invisible oxide skin that stops rust.

name: Bronze
note: Copper plus tin. Harder than either metal alone, it gave the Bronze Age its name.

name: Brass
note: Copper plus zinc: golden, easy to shape, and great for instruments and fittings.

name: Sterling silver
note: Pure silver is too soft for daily use, so a little copper is added for strength.

name: 14k gold
note: 14 parts out of 24 are gold. The rest varies by jeweler; this is a typical yellow-gold mix.

name: Solder
note: A common lead-free solder that melts around 217 °C to join parts on circuit boards.

name: US penny
note: Since 1982, pennies are a zinc core with a thin copper coat.

name: US nickel (5¢ coin)
note: Despite its name, a nickel coin is mostly copper.

name: US quarter / dime
note: A copper core sandwiched between copper-nickel layers; look at the edge to see the copper stripe.

name: Pewter
note: Modern lead-free pewter: mostly tin, hardened with antimony and copper.

name: Soda can
note: An aluminum alloy; small amounts of manganese and magnesium make the thin walls strong.

name: Aluminum foil
note: Nearly pure aluminum rolled very thin. People still call it 'tin foil' because it once really was tin.

name: Light-bulb filament
note: Tungsten, chosen because it melts at 3,422 °C, hotter than any other metal.

name: Gunpowder (black powder)
note: A historic mix of saltpeter, charcoal and sulfur. Shown for chemistry only.
